01 / Research proposition Research framework

What changes when we treat governance as something we can compose, inspect and contest?

Physical environments are governed through intertwined relationships: access, capacity, authority, dependency and public claims. Coupling Space is an experimental way to make those relationships visible and to ask who bears the consequences when they change.

Represent the situationTest a transformationChallenge the assumptions
02 / Research architecture Research framework

One inquiry. Three connected practices.

From relational theory to computational experiment to public interpretation.

I / THEORY

Coupling Space

Start with a place and the relationships that hold it together: routes, utilities, people, machines, rules and shared resources. Map what depends on what, where constraints apply, and which changes become possible when one part moves or fails.

II / EXPERIMENT

Composition Lab

Change one part of the arrangement and compare the results with the starting point. The lab records what was moved, which assumptions were used, and how the effects are distributed, so anyone can check the numbers for themselves.

III / CIVIC PRACTICE

Social Synthesis

Give people a shared way to describe what they see, suggest another arrangement and question the model itself. A calculation shows consequences under stated assumptions. Questions of fairness, of whose account counts and of what a community will accept stay with the people involved.

06 / Computational reference Working prototype

The smallest Python experiment unit

The page and coupling_state.py compute the same object: the stiffness structure of the coupling space, independent of how much resource it holds.

Geometry enters the state

Physical couplings weaken with distance and institutional ones keep their weight. Moving an object changes only the former.

Placement over amount

After the power anchor is lost, moving the same 1.2 of reserve restores the protected minimum from 0.444 to 0.825, above the starting 0.600.

Verifiable

The leverage formula is checked against finite differences, and state records reproduce exactly, with any change altering the hash.

Checking parity with the Python reference…
python -m pip install numpy
python coupling_state.py              # runs S0 → S1 → S2, writes reference.json
python -m unittest -v test_coupling_state.py   # 10 tests

Φ_G(v) = 1 / [K⁻¹]ᵥᵥ, where K is the grounded stiffness matrix. Reserve is held as backup anchorage, so losing the power anchor softens K, and moving the reserve re-places the prestress.

07 / Composition Lab: geometric proofs Working prototype

Proving a place kept its rules, with the data kept local

Most spatial computing systems find out whether a place is working by watching it. Sensors stream data into a central model, and the model is checked afterwards. The Composition Lab is testing a different route. The boundaries, capacities and adjacencies of a place are written as rules in a zero-knowledge circuit. When something moves through that place, the operator produces a short proof that every rule held.

A regulator or a resident can check the proof and see the outcome, while the raw operating data stays with whoever holds it. Space becomes the constraint system: the physical arrangement decides which actions can be proved.

Continuous telemetry (digital twins) Geometric proof (Coupling Space)
System state A live 3D model kept current by constant IoT updates. Rules derived from the physical layout, checked at the moment an action happens.
Transactions Database events that modify a central model. Flows across nodes, each producing a proof.
Data and GDPR Continuous streams that are retained and can be used for tracking. Only what the proof needs, held locally by the operator.
Infrastructure Dense edge gateways and streaming pipelines. Proofs generated on local hardware and checked quickly and cheaply.
Governance Automated loops that are hard to inspect. Machines produce proofs; people judge what the rules should be.
  1. Audit sheet and workbenchDescribe the situation, what must hold, and where the reserve sits.
  2. Prover.tomlThe current state is exported as circuit inputs, with private and public values kept apart.
  3. Noir circuitnargo execute checks every assertion. If one fails, no proof can be made.
  4. Proof and public outputsBarretenberg writes the proof file. Only the floor, the total and the record reference are public.
  5. VerificationChecked on Ethereum or an enterprise ledger, or by a civic auditor directly in a browser.

A toy circuit that matches the workbench

Noir is an open-source language for zero-knowledge programs, developed by Aztec Labs, with syntax close to Rust. It compiles to an intermediate form called ACIR, so the same circuit can run on different proving backends. The circuit below proves that every protected element stays at or above the floor the community set, and that the reserve adds up to the declared total, without revealing any single element’s value.

// coupling_floor/src/main.nr
global N: u32 = 10;   // elements on the grid street
global R: u32 = 5;    // sites that can hold reserve

fn main(
    phi_milli: [u64; N],          // private: effective stiffness × 1000
    reserve_milli: [u64; R],      // private: reserve at each site × 1000
    protected: pub [bool; N],      // public: which elements must hold
    floor_milli: pub u64,          // public: the agreed floor × 1000
    reserve_total_milli: pub u64,  // public: declared reserve total
    record_ref: pub Field,         // public: stamped record it refers to
) {
    for i in 0..N {
        if protected[i] {
            assert(phi_milli[i] >= floor_milli);
        }
    }
    let mut total: u64 = 0;
    for i in 0..R { total += reserve_milli[i]; }
    assert(total == reserve_total_milli);
    assert(record_ref != 0);
}

Export from the current state

Every change you make in the workbench updates the check below. The exported Prover.toml drops straight into a Noir project for nargo execute and bb prove.

Why European institutions are paying attention

eIDAS 2.0 and the EU Digital Identity Wallet
The wallet is being rolled out across member states so people can prove identity, residence, qualifications or age across borders. It already supports sharing selected attributes. Zero-knowledge proofs go further: a holder can show that a claim is true, such as being over 18, without revealing a birth date or leaving a trail that links one use to the next.
Data minimisation under the GDPR
Article 5(1)(c) of the GDPR asks organisations to process only the data a purpose requires. Continuous telemetry sits uneasily with that principle. A proof carries only what verification needs.
EBSI and cross-border verification
The European Blockchain Services Infrastructure is built to verify credentials issued by public bodies, supply-chain provenance and carbon data across borders. Zero-knowledge proofs let agencies in each member state check these independently, with sensitive data staying where it was issued.

ÉTÈ extends the idea to physical systems

Most EU zero-knowledge work today focuses on identity: proving who someone is. ÉTÈ focuses on proving what happened in a place.

From identity to infrastructure
Showing that a transport network, a green-energy microgrid or a municipal land-use transaction met its legal, environmental and spatial rules, using proofs in place of cameras and raw telemetry.
Auditable and privacy-preserving
Giving civic auditors a proof they can inspect, confirming that an urban or industrial process followed public policy while operational details remain confidential.

Questions we are working on

A proof is as trustworthy as its inputs. The circuit shows that the rules hold if the values are true, and those values come from sensors, operators or inspectors. We are working on how to have those inputs signed by a trusted party, how to bind the record reference to a hash computed inside the circuit, and how to turn spatial adjacency, for example DGGS grid cells, into reusable circuit libraries.

Track A

Noir circuits

Writing spatial geometry, network adjacency and capacity limits as reusable Noir circuit libraries.

Track B

Audit interfaces

Connecting spatial modelling workbenches to readable composition audit sheets and verifiable outputs.

Track C

Civic research

Studying privacy-conscious proof architectures for public infrastructure and institutional governance.

08 / Geometric cryptography Working prototype

Geometric cryptography: the composition is the proof

Move the infrastructure. The rules of the space decide what can be proved, and a verifier learns that the rules held, while every position stays with you.

On the left is the operator’s full composition. On the right is everything a verifier receives. The two views rotate together. The spiked crystal floating above is the commitment itself: the 32 bytes of the Merkle root, one spine per byte, each spine as long as its byte’s value. Move any element and it changes shape, while revealing no position.

Operator · private witness
Verifier · public only

Public rules

These parameters go into the public statement. Both sides see them.

Your witness

Select an element on the left. Its position and throughput exist only on this device.

Commitment and verdict

01 · Space as the circuit

Boundaries and capacities are the constraints

The boundary cell, the throughput limit and the coupling length become assertions directly. The spatial arrangement decides which statements can be proved.

02 · Commitment in place of collection

One root stands for the whole witness

Each element is salted and hashed into a leaf, and the leaves combine into a Merkle root. The verifier holds the root. Any change alters it, and the root itself reveals no position.

03 · Selective disclosure

Open only the one that is asked for

When an audit calls for it, the operator opens a single element with its Merkle path. The verifier confirms it belongs to the committed composition, and the rest stay sealed.

Commitments, Merkle paths and checks on this page are computed for real in your browser, and nothing is sent anywhere. The rule check runs on this device. In the full pipeline the same statement is proved by a Noir zero-knowledge circuit, like the one on the Proofs page, so the verifier does not need to trust the operator’s device.

09 / Quantum-safe governance Working prototype

Signed for decades: quantum-safe mandates and records

Streets, grids and municipal robots stay in service for thirty years or more. The mandates that govern them, and the records of what they did, need to stay trustworthy for the whole of that time, including after quantum computers can break the signature schemes in common use today.

Here you can sign the composition from the workbench with the post-quantum signature standards NIST published in 2024. The signature covers the whole arrangement: the protected elements, the floor, where the reserve sits and where every element stands. Change any of it after signing and the signature stops verifying.

Mandate under signature

Read live from the workbench. Change something there, then come back and see whether the signature still holds.

Change it in the workbench

Signer

The key is generated in this browser tab for demonstration. In a deployment it would be held by a qualified trust service provider.

Record chain hashes

SHA-256. Quantum search at most halves its strength to about 128 bits, which is sufficient now and later.

Ready

Mandate signatures

ML-DSA (lattice-based) or SLH-DSA (hash-based), in place of ECDSA, which Shor’s algorithm breaks.

Running on this page

Long-horizon records

Seal the chain head, and re-seal under newer algorithms as standards change, so records stay verifiable for the life of the asset.

Running on this page

Spatial constraint proofs

The Noir circuit on the Proofs page currently runs on the Barretenberg backend, which is built on the BN254 curve and is classical. The next step is a hash-based (FRI) proving backend, with the circuit itself unchanged.

In transition

A mandate you can inspect

Authorisation is written as a signed file that states what is allowed, where, and who approved it. The enforcement point checks it before an action happens, and acts only on a mandate whose signature verifies.

Records that outlast the hardware

For signatures, the long-term risk is that someone later forges or backdates an old record. Post-quantum signatures plus regular re-sealing keep an audit sound twenty or thirty years on.

Geometry says what, cryptography protects it

The spatial arrangement decides which actions are allowed and which rules must hold. Post-quantum signatures and proofs make sure those rules, and the record of keeping them, cannot be altered or forged.

The EU’s coordinated implementation roadmap (June 2025) asks member states to have national post-quantum plans by the end of 2026, to migrate high-risk uses such as critical infrastructure by 2030, and to complete as much of the rest as feasible by 2035.

ÉTÈ’s mandate and record formats are designed for that timeline from the start, with room to move to newer algorithms as standards change.

10 / Future applications Research direction

From the street to the Moon

A lunar settlement can be designed across one site, three phases (years 1, 10 and 20) and three scales: the human and robot, the building, and neighbourhood infrastructure. The same state grammar can describe how a settlement’s power, pressurised volume and access couplings hold across those scales, and how a lost anchor propagates between them.

This is a direction ÉTÈ plans to develop in 2027.
